knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb Z^A,\ l\le x\le u}\left\{g(\partial x)+\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a)\right\}.\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the M-convex submodular-flow container, but no source supports the precise objective, domain conventions, terminology, or the claim that an indicator of integral base-polyhedron points recovers the stated submodular boundary model.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonintegral boundary data can destroy integral-flow feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the one-arc digraph \(s\to t\) with \(0\le x_a\le1\) and require \(\partial x=(-1/2,1/2)\). The unique feasible flow is \(x_a=1/2\), so the feasible polyhedron contains no integral flow despite integral arc bounds. Thus an integrality theorem for submodular flows cannot generally survive replacement of an integral base-polyhedron boundary by arbitrary nonintegral boundary data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral capacities do not guarantee an integral flow when the prescribed boundary or its defining polyhedron is nonintegral.
assumptions_latex: The boundary convention is net inflow.
The boundary requirement is the singleton \(\{(-1/2,1/2)\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\{x\in[0,1]:\partial x=(-1/2,1/2)\}=\{1/2\},\qquad \{1/2\}\cap\mathbb Z=\varnothing.\]

notation.meaning: Flow on the sole arc from s to t.
Net inflow boundary vector ordered as s,t.

source_refs.locator: Section 12. Integrality of Flows and the Unimodular Property p. 160

source_witnesses.locator: Section 12. Integrality of Flows and the Unimodular Property p. 160

knowledge_statements.title: Incompatible Boundary Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous boundary requirements may make a flow model infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{s,t\}\) and impose simultaneously \(\partial x\in B_1\) and \(\partial x\in B_2\), where \(B_1=\{(-1,1)\}\) and \(B_2=\{(1,-1)\}\). Each boundary system is individually feasible on a suitably oriented unit arc, but \(B_1\cap B_2=\varnothing\). Consequently no flow on any common network can satisfy both boundary requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two individually meaningful boundary systems can be mutually inconsistent because their feasible boundary sets have empty intersection.
assumptions_latex: Both boundary constraints apply to the same boundary vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[B_1\cap B_2=\varnothing\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \{x:\partial x\in B_1,\ \partial x\in B_2\}=\varnothing.\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The empty-intersection implication is directly correct and the failure_boundary kind fits, but the record has no evidence for treating these singleton sets as the relevant boundary systems in the local neoflow model. A source defining or analyzing simultaneous boundary systems is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonseparable-Cost Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cross-arc interactions cannot generally be encoded by unary arc costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On two binary arc variables, let \(C(x_1,x_2)=x_1x_2\). If \(C\) admitted a separable representation \(C(x_1,x_2)=\phi_1(x_1)+\phi_2(x_2)\), its rectangular mixed difference would vanish. Instead, \(C(1,1)-C(1,0)-C(0,1)+C(0,0)=1\). Hence this interaction cost cannot be represented by separable arc costs without auxiliary variables or an enlarged state space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A genuine interaction between arc variables defeats a sum of unary arc costs unless the formulation is enlarged.
assumptions_latex: A separable representation uses only one unary function per variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C(x_1,x_2)=x_1x_2\ne\phi_1(x_1)+\phi_2(x_2)\quad\text{for all choices of }\phi_1,\phi_2.\]

notation.meaning: Joint cost of the two arc variables.
Hypothetical unary cost for variable i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mixed-difference calculation correctly rules out a sum of two unary costs for the displayed binary interaction, and failure_boundary is the proper kind. No source is supplied for the broader modeling conclusion concerning auxiliary variables or enlarged state spaces.

children.title: Value-Oracle Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Limitations arising from oracle-based access to flow-model data.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Oracle Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete recovery from a value oracle has exponential query cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be accessible only through a value oracle returning \(f(S)\) for a queried \(S\subseteq V\). Any procedure required to output the complete value table of an otherwise unrestricted member of a full-dimensional submodular family must query every unqueried coordinate in the worst case. Thus complete explicit recovery requires \(2^{|V|}\) oracle calls, although particular optimization tasks may require far fewer calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value oracle avoids storing an exponential table, but reconstructing the entire submodular function still requires exponentially many queries.
assumptions_latex: The oracle returns one exact set value per call.
The required output is the complete table.
The admissible submodular family has freely perturbable coordinates locally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Q_{\mathrm{table}}(|V|)\ge 2^{|V|}.\]

notation.meaning: Worst-case oracle queries needed to recover the complete table.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A complexity bound is appropriate for this container, but the exact 2^{|V|} lower bound depends on a formally specified oracle, algorithmic, and admissible-family model. The phrase freely perturbable coordinates locally does not by itself establish the adversarial indistinguishability claim, and no source is cited.

children.title: Explicit Representation Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Limitations arising from explicit descriptions of feasible structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Representation Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tabular representation grows exponentially with the ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An explicit value-table representation of \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) stores one entry for each subset of \(V\). Therefore it contains exactly \(2^{|V|}\) entries. If every value is represented with \(b\) bits, the table occupies \(2^{|V|}b\) bits, before indexing overhead. Submodularity inequalities restrict admissible tables but do not change the number of coordinates in this representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Listing every value of a set function uses exponentially many entries, even when the function is submodular.
assumptions_latex: The representation lists every subset value explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{size}_{\mathrm{table}}(f)=2^{|V|}b\ \text{ bits}.\]

notation.meaning: Bits used for one stored function value.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counting statement is correct for the explicitly stipulated full value table, and complexity_bound fits the terminal container. However, there is no citation or explicit standard-field rationale record supporting the representation-complexity claim; the review flag alone is not an inspectable rationale.

children.title: Succinct Encoding Limits
children.top_down_role: Failure boundaries associated with compressed input descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Succinct Encoding Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Succinct encodings necessarily cover only structured subfamilies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n=|V|\), a code of length at most \(p(n)\) bits has at most \(2^{p(n)+1}-1\) distinct codewords. Consequently, if a finite class \(\mathcal F_n\) of exactly represented submodular functions satisfies \(|\mathcal F_n|>2^{p(n)+1}-1\), no injective encoding of all members can use at most \(p(n)\) bits. Polynomial-size formulas therefore require structural restrictions and cannot encode every sufficiently large finite submodular class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-bit format has too few codewords to represent every member of a sufficiently large submodular family exactly.
assumptions_latex: Exact representation requires distinct functions to have distinct decodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[|\mathcal F_n|>2^{p(n)+1}-1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\max_{f\in\mathcal F_n}\operatorname{length}(\operatorname{enc}(f))>p(n).\]

notation.meaning: Finite class of submodular functions on an n-element ground set.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-codeword counting implication is valid for injective exact binary encodings, and failure_boundary fits the container. The claimed consequence for submodular functions remains conditional because no sufficiently large submodular family is instantiated or sourced, and the meaning of formula encoding is not formalized.

children.title: Generalized Submodular Domains
children.top_down_role: Classical extensions of set-function submodularity to restricted families, lattices, signed domains, and multilabel domains, including their polyhedral and optimization interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersecting-Submodular Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Submodularity restricted to pairs having nonempty intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and let \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^V\) satisfy \(X\cap Y,X\cup Y\in\mathcal F\) whenever \(X,Y\in\mathcal F\) and \(X\cap Y\ne\varnothing\). A function \(f:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\) is intersecting-submodular if, for every such intersecting pair, \(f(X)+f(Y)\ge f(X\cap Y)+f(X\cup Y)\). No inequality is required by this definition for disjoint pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting submodularity imposes the usual submodular inequality only on domain pairs with nonempty intersection.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is closed under union and intersection of intersecting pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[X,Y\in\mathcal F,\ X\cap Y\ne\varnothing\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(X)+f(Y)\ge f(X\cap Y)+f(X\cup Y).\]

notation.meaning: Intersecting family forming the function domain.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the terminal container and the displayed inequality is internally consistent. Because conventions differ between functions on all of 2^V and functions on intersecting families with closure assumptions, an authoritative source with a precise definition locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Crossing-Submodular Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-family formulation with closure required only for crossing pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite. Two sets \(X,Y\subseteq V\) cross if \(X\cap Y\), \(X\setminus Y\), \(Y\setminus X\), and \(V\setminus(X\cup Y)\) are all nonempty. A pair \((\mathcal F,f)\), where \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^V\) and \(f:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\), is a crossing-submodular system if, whenever \(X,Y\in\mathcal F\) cross, both \(X\cap Y,X\cup Y\in\mathcal F\) and \[f(X)+f(Y)\ge f(X\cap Y)+f(X\cup Y).\] No inequality or closure condition is imposed on noncrossing pairs by this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A crossing-submodular system is closed under union and intersection of crossing members, and its function satisfies the submodular inequality on exactly those pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X,Y\in\mathcal F\) crossing implies \(X\cap Y,X\cup Y\in\mathcal F\) and \(f(X)+f(Y)\ge f(X\cap Y)+f(X\cup Y)\).

notation.meaning: restricted family of subsets of the ground set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no citation establishes the intended crossing convention or the combined closure-and-inequality terminology.

children.title: Cross-Free Representations
children.top_down_role: Representations organized by cross-free constraint families.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Free Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of compatible bipartitions by arbitrarily oriented shores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite. A split is an unordered bipartition \(\{A,V\setminus A\}\) with \(\varnothing\ne A\ne V\). A cross-free representation of a split family \(\mathcal S\) chooses one shore \(A_s\) from every \(s\in\mathcal S\) such that no two chosen shores cross. Equivalently, for every \(s,t\in\mathcal S\), at least one of the four intersections of a shore of \(s\) with a shore of \(t\) is empty. Replacing any \(A_s\) by \(V\setminus A_s\) changes its orientation but represents the same split.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cross-free representation chooses one shore of each split so that every pair of represented bipartitions has an empty corner.
assumptions_latex: Every split has two nonempty shores.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal S=\{\{A_s,V\setminus A_s\}:s\in\mathcal S\}\) with the chosen shores pairwise noncrossing.

notation.meaning: family of splits of the ground set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits, but a source is needed to confirm that the leaf concerns compatible splits represented by oriented shores. The conclusion also reuses s both as an index and as a member of the split family.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tree Representations of Cross-Free and Laminar Set Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of cross-free families by tree representations and of laminar families by arborescence representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(U,\mathcal F)$ be a set system. If $(T,\varphi)$ is a tree representation of $(U,\mathcal F)$, then $\mathcal F$ is cross-free. If, moreover, $T$ is an arborescence, then $\mathcal F$ is laminar. Conversely, every cross-free family has a tree representation, and every laminar family has a tree representation in which $T$ can be chosen to be an arborescence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree-representable set system is cross-free, and an arborescence-representable set system is laminar. Conversely, every cross-free family has a tree representation, and every laminar family has an arborescence representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F\text{ is cross-free}\iff (U,\mathcal F)\text{ has a tree representation},\qquad \mathcal F\text{ is laminar}\iff (U,\mathcal F)\text{ has an arborescence representation}.

source_evidence.locator: Graphs / 2.2. Trees, Circuits, and Cuts / Proposition 2.14

source_refs.locator: Graphs / 2.2. Trees, Circuits, and Cuts / Proposition 2.14

source_witnesses.locator: Graphs / 2.2. Trees, Circuits, and Cuts / Proposition 2.14

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cardinality Bounds for Laminar and Cross-Free Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear upper bounds for families of distinct subsets of a finite ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $U$ be finite. A laminar family $\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U$ of distinct subsets satisfies $|\mathcal F|\le 2|U|$. A cross-free family $\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U$ of distinct subsets satisfies $|\mathcal F|\le 4|U|-2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A laminar family of distinct subsets of a finite set U has at most 2|U| members, while a cross-free family of distinct subsets has at most 4|U|−2 members.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\text{ is a family of distinct subsets}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F\text{ laminar}\Rightarrow |\mathcal F|\le 2|U|,\qquad \mathcal F\text{ cross-free}\Rightarrow |\mathcal F|\le 4|U|-2.

source_evidence.locator: Graphs / 2.2. Trees, Circuits, and Cuts / Corollary 2.15

children.title: Laminar Representations
children.top_down_role: Representations organized by nested constraint families.

knowledge_statements.title: Laminar Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Root-oriented representation of a compatible split family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and fix a root \(r\in V\). A laminar representation of a split family \(\mathcal S\) is a family \(\mathcal L\subseteq 2^{V\setminus\{r\}}\) containing exactly one shore of each split, with \(r\) excluded, such that for all \(A,B\in\mathcal L\), \[A\subseteq B,\qquad B\subseteq A,\qquad\text{or}\qquad A\cap B=\varnothing.\] Thus inclusion among represented shores forms a forest, while disjoint shores occupy separate branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orient every split away from a root. The representation is laminar when any two selected shores are nested or disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L\) contains one root-free shore per split and is laminar under inclusion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The root-oriented laminar representation is precise and appropriately classified, but no inspectable source supports this exact split-representation convention.

children.title: Cross-Free-to-Laminar Reduction
children.top_down_role: Structural routes from cross-free descriptions to laminar descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Free-to-Laminar Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Root orientation converts compatible splits into a laminar shore family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite, let \(\mathcal S\) be a cross-free family of splits, and fix \(r\in V\). For each split \(s=\{A,V\setminus A\}\), let \(L_s\) be its unique shore not containing \(r\). Then \(\mathcal L_r=\{L_s:s\in\mathcal S\}\) is laminar. Moreover, \(s\mapsto L_s\) is injective and the original splits are recovered by \(s=\{L_s,V\setminus L_s\}\). Hence root orientation preserves the represented bipartitions while replacing a cross-free representation by a laminar one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing the shore not containing a fixed root turns every cross-free split family into a laminar family without losing any split.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal S\) is a cross-free family of nontrivial splits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L_r=\{L_s:s\in\mathcal S\}\) is laminar and \(s=\{L_s,V\setminus L_s\}\).

notation.meaning: shore of split s that excludes the root

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role and conclusion fit the reduction leaf, but the result depends on the exact meaning of a cross-free split family, for which no source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributive-Lattice Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Submodularity on finite distributive lattices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((L,\wedge,\vee)\) be a finite distributive lattice. A function \(f:L\to\mathbb R\) is lattice-submodular if, for every \(x,y\in L\), \[f(x)+f(y)\ge f(x\wedge y)+f(x\vee y).\] When \(L=2^V\), meet and join are intersection and union, so this definition specializes to ordinary set-function submodularity. Distributivity means that meet and join distribute over one another, for example \(x\wedge(y\vee z)=(x\wedge y)\vee(x\wedge z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function on a finite distributive lattice is submodular when its values dominate the sum at the meet and join of every pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)+f(y)\ge f(x\wedge y)+f(x\vee y)\) for all \(x,y\in L\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The standard finite distributive-lattice definition is internally correct and fits the node, but it has no citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Poset-Ideal Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Birkhoff representation for finite distributive lattices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be a finite distributive lattice and let \(P=J(L)\) be the poset of join-irreducible elements of \(L\). For \(x\in L\), define \(I_x=\{p\in P:p\le x\}\). Then \(I_x\) is an order ideal, and \[x\longmapsto I_x\] is a lattice isomorphism from \(L\) onto the ideal lattice \(\mathcal I(P)\), where meet and join correspond respectively to intersection and union. Its inverse maps an ideal \(I\) to \(\bigvee_{p\in I}p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite distributive lattice is isomorphic to the lattice of order ideals of its poset of join-irreducible elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\cong\mathcal I(J(L))\), with \(I_{x\wedge y}=I_x\cap I_y\) and \(I_{x\vee y}=I_x\cup I_y\).

notation.meaning: poset of join-irreducible elements of L
family of order ideals of P

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the standard finite Birkhoff representation and the representation kind fits, but no authoritative source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Lattice-Minimization Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction from distributive-lattice minimization to submodular minimization over ideals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite distributive lattice \(L\), a value oracle for a submodular \(f:L\to\mathbb R\), and its ideal representation \(x\mapsto I_x\subseteq P=J(L)\). Define \(g:\mathcal I(P)\to\mathbb R\) by \(g(I_x)=f(x)\), and extend it by \(\widetilde g(S)=g(S)\) for ideals and \(\widetilde g(S)=+\infty\) otherwise. Minimize the extended-valued submodular function \(\widetilde g\) over \(2^P\) with a submodular-minimization method. Output the lattice element corresponding to any minimizing ideal \(I^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent lattice elements as poset ideals, forbid nonideals with infinite cost, minimize the resulting submodular set function, and map the optimal ideal back.
assumptions_latex: A value oracle and the ideal representation are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*=\bigvee_{p\in I^*}p\) satisfies \(f(x^*)=\min_{x\in L}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: extended-valued set-function encoding of the lattice objective

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction is plausible, but a source must verify that the extended-valued encoding is submodular in the adopted framework and that the invoked minimization method accepts infinite values or provides a valid finite-value replacement.

knowledge_statements.title: Bisubmodular Function Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard signed-set definition on disjoint pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite set \(V\), let \(3^V=\{(X,Y):X,Y\subseteq V,\ X\cap Y=\varnothing\}\). Define \((X,Y)\sqcap(X',Y')=(X\cap X',Y\cap Y')\) and \[(X,Y)\sqcup(X',Y')=\bigl((X\cup X')\setminus(Y\cup Y'),(Y\cup Y')\setminus(X\cup X')\bigr).\] A function \(f:3^V\to\mathbb R\) is bisubmodular if, for all \(p,q\in3^V\), \[f(p)+f(q)\ge f(p\sqcap q)+f(p\sqcup q).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bisubmodular function is defined on disjoint signed set pairs and satisfies the submodular inequality using signed meet and reduced union.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(p)+f(q)\ge f(p\sqcap q)+f(p\sqcup q)\) for every \(p,q\in3^V\).

notation.meaning: domain of ordered disjoint subset pairs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The signed-pair definition is internally consistent and fits the function-class leaf, but no source confirms the adopted meet and reduced-union convention.

children.title: Bisubmodular Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Geometric structure associated with bisubmodular systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Bisubmodular Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedron associated with a normalized bisubmodular function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:3^V\to\mathbb R\) be bisubmodular with \(f(\varnothing,\varnothing)=0\). For \(x\in\mathbb R^V\), write \(x(X)=\sum_{i\in X}x_i\). The bisubmodular polyhedron of \(f\) is \[P(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^V:x(X)-x(Y)\le f(X,Y)\text{ for every }(X,Y)\in3^V\}.\] Its defining inequalities are indexed by signed subsets, with positive coordinates selected by \(X\) and negative coordinates selected by \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bisubmodular polyhedron consists of vectors whose signed sum over every disjoint pair is at most the corresponding function value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^V:x(X)-x(Y)\le f(X,Y)\ \forall(X,Y)\in3^V\}\).

notation.meaning: sum of coordinates indexed by X

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent and appropriately classified, but the precise normalization and signed-inequality convention require an authoritative citation.

children.title: Signed Greedy Geometry
children.top_down_role: Signed ordering structure within bisubmodular geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Signed Greedy Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed greedy construction for linear optimization over a bisubmodular polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(w\in\mathbb R^V\), order \(V\) as \(i_1,\ldots,i_n\) so that \(|w_{i_1}|\ge\cdots\ge|w_{i_n}|\). Initialize \((A_0,B_0)=(\varnothing,\varnothing)\). At step \(k\), add \(i_k\) to \(A_{k-1}\) if \(w_{i_k}\ge0\), and to \(B_{k-1}\) otherwise, obtaining \((A_k,B_k)\). Set \[x_{i_k}=\operatorname{sgn}(w_{i_k})\bigl(f(A_k,B_k)-f(A_{k-1},B_{k-1})\bigr),\] using either sign when \(w_{i_k}=0\), and output \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order elements by absolute weight, grow a signed chain according to weight signs, and assign signed marginal function increments to coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The construction outputs a signed-chain vector \(x\) associated with \(w\) and \(f\).

notation.meaning: signed prefix pair after k greedy steps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic construction fits the leaf, but no source verifies the marginal rule and zero-weight convention. The record also stops short of stating the principal guarantee that the output is feasible for the associated polyhedron.

children.title: Polyhedral–Greedy Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The interface linking bisubmodular polyhedra to signed greedy structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral–Greedy Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-function characterization for the bisubmodular polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:3^V\to\mathbb R\) be normalized and bisubmodular, and let \(P(f)\) be its bisubmodular polyhedron. For \(w\in\mathbb R^V\), form the signed chain \((A_k,B_k)\) by nonincreasing \(|w_i|\), and put \(\lambda_k=|w_{i_k}|-|w_{i_{k+1}}|\), where \(|w_{i_{n+1}}|=0\). Then the signed greedy vector attains \[\max_{x\in P(f)}w^\mathsf T x=\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k f(A_k,B_k).\] Thus signed greedy marginal vectors expose supporting faces of \(P(f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear optimization over a bisubmodular polyhedron equals a weighted sum of function values along the signed greedy chain.
assumptions_latex: \(P(f)\) is defined by all signed-set inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{x\in P(f)}w^\mathsf T x=\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_k f(A_k,B_k)\), attained by the signed greedy vector.

notation.meaning: successive difference of ordered absolute weights

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed support-function equality is mathematically specific and cannot be validated from the supplied inventory. A source should also clarify whether this correspondence is best treated as a theorem/property rather than duality.

knowledge_statements.title: Bisubmodular Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-oracle tractability of finite bisubmodular minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:3^V\to\mathbb Q\) be bisubmodular and supplied by a value oracle, with \(n=|V|\) and oracle values having encoding length at most \(L\). The optimization problem \[\min\{f(X,Y):(X,Y)\in3^V\}\] admits an exact algorithm using a number of arithmetic operations and oracle calls polynomial in \(n\) and \(L\). The output is a disjoint pair \((X^*,Y^*)\) attaining the minimum; no enumeration of all \(3^n\) signed subsets is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational-valued bisubmodular function can be minimized exactly in polynomial oracle time over all disjoint signed set pairs.
assumptions_latex: A value oracle with polynomially encoded outputs is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An exact minimizer \((X^*,Y^*)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{(X,Y)\in3^V}f(X,Y)\) is computable in time polynomial in \(n\) and \(L\).

notation.meaning: maximum binary encoding length of an oracle value

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the claim, but exact polynomial-time bisubmodular minimization and its dependence on n and L require a specific theorem citation and a precise oracle/arithmetic complexity model.

knowledge_statements.title: k-Submodular Function Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard star-domain definition for finite-valued functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D_k=\{0,1,\ldots,k\}\), where \(0\) is a distinguished null label. For \(a,b\in D_k\), define \(a\sqcap b=a\) when \(a=b\), and \(a\sqcap b=0\) otherwise; define \(a\sqcup b=a\) when \(b=0\), \(a\sqcup b=b\) when \(a=0\), \(a\sqcup b=a\) when \(a=b\), and \(a\sqcup b=0\) otherwise. Extend both operations coordinatewise to \(D_k^V\). A function \(f:D_k^V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is \(k\)-submodular if
\[f(x)+f(y)\ge f(x\sqcap y)+f(x\sqcup y)\qquad(x,y\in D_k^V).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A k-submodular function satisfies the submodular inequality under the meet and join operations of a star-shaped label domain with one null label.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)+f(y)\ge f(x\sqcap y)+f(x\sqcup y)\) for all \(x,y\in D_k^V\).

notation.meaning: The star label domain with null label 0 and k nonnull labels.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and selected content kind fit the k-submodular function-class container, and the star-domain operations are mathematically standard. No source reference or inspectable locator is supplied, so the claim cannot pass candidate review.

children.title: Multilabel Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Relaxation structures used for multilabel submodular problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Multilabel Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-polytope relaxation of a finite pairwise multilabel energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), label set \(L\), and energy \(F(x)=\sum_{i\in V}\theta_i(x_i)+\sum_{ij\in E}\theta_{ij}(x_i,x_j)\), its local-polytope relaxation minimizes
\[\sum_{i,a}\theta_i(a)\mu_i(a)+\sum_{ij,a,b}\theta_{ij}(a,b)\mu_{ij}(a,b)\]
over nonnegative variables satisfying \(\sum_a\mu_i(a)=1\), \(\sum_b\mu_{ij}(a,b)=\mu_i(a)\), and \(\sum_a\mu_{ij}(a,b)=\mu_j(b)\). Every labeling \(x\in L^V\) embeds through the integral marginals \(\mu_i(a)=\mathbf 1[a=x_i]\) and \(\mu_{ij}(a,b)=\mathbf 1[(a,b)=(x_i,x_j)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local-polytope relaxation replaces each labeling by consistent node and edge marginals, retaining every integral labeling while permitting fractional solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxed optimum is no greater than \(\min_{x\in L^V}F(x)\).

notation.meaning: Relaxed marginal assigning label a to vertex i.
Relaxed joint marginal on edge ij.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local-polytope definition fits the relaxation container and correctly embeds integral labelings, but the summation and constraint domains for a and b should be made explicit. More importantly, the record has no source or locator supporting the formulation.

children.title: Multilabel Representations
children.top_down_role: Encoding structures for multilabel submodular objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Multilabel Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of star-domain labelings by disjoint set tuples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D_k=\{0,1,\ldots,k\}\). Each labeling \(x\in D_k^V\) corresponds bijectively to the ordered tuple \((X_1,\ldots,X_k)\), where \(X_ell=\{i\in V:x_i=\ell\}\); the sets are pairwise disjoint, and coordinates outside \(\bigcup_{ell=1}^kX_ell\) receive label \(0\). Under this correspondence, coordinatewise \(k\)-submodular meet and join become
\[(X\sqcap Y)_ell=X_ell\cap Y_ell,\qquad (X\sqcup Y)_ell=(X_ell\cup Y_ell)\setminus\bigcup_{m\neell}(X_m\cup Y_m).\]
Thus a function on \(D_k^V\) has an equivalent representation on ordered pairwise-disjoint \(k\)-tuples of subsets of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multilabel assignment is equivalently an ordered tuple of disjoint label classes; the null label consists of elements in none of those classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_k^V\) is in bijection with the pairwise-disjoint tuples \((X_1,\ldots,X_k)\).

notation.meaning: Set of elements assigned nonnull label ell.
Null label 0 together with k nonnull labels.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A disjoint-set-tuple representation is appropriate for this container, but occurrences of X_ell should be X_\ell, and \neell is an undefined command that should be \ne \ell. No cited source supports the representation convention or the induced operations.

children.title: Relaxation–Representation Fidelity
children.top_down_role: Exactness gaps between multilabel objects, relaxations, plus encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation–Representation Fidelity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness criterion for a relaxation linked to a labeling representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:L^V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), let \(P\) be a relaxation domain, let \(\iota:L^V\to P\) encode labelings, and let \(\bar F:P\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). The pair \((P,\bar F)\) is faithful for minimization of \(F\) when
\[\bar F(\iota(x))=F(x)\quad(x\in L^V),\qquad \min_{z\in P}\bar F(z)=\min_{x\in L^V}F(x),\]
and at least one relaxed minimizer belongs to \(\iota(L^V)\). It is fully faithful when every relaxed minimizer lies in \(\iota(L^V)\), so decoding introduces neither an objective gap nor an extraneous fractional optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A representation-relaxation pair is faithful when it preserves integral energies and has an integral optimum with exactly the original minimum value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Faithfulness is equivalent to value exactness together with existence of an encoded relaxed minimizer.

notation.meaning: Embedding of discrete labelings into the relaxation domain.
Relaxed objective extending the discrete energy.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition content kind fits the fidelity container, but “faithful” and “fully faithful” are project-local terminology requiring an explicit source or declared convention. On the stated finite discrete domain, extension equality plus value exactness makes some of the minimizer conditions redundant when minima are attained, so the intended distinction also needs authoritative alignment.

children.title: Multilabel Minimization
children.top_down_role: Optimization scope for multilabel submodular objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Multilabel Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain minimization with explicit label and oracle conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite ground set \(V\), a finite label set \(L\), and a function \(F:L^V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), the multilabel minimization problem is
\[F^*=\min_{x\in L^V}F(x),\qquad X^*=\{x\in L^V:F(x)=F^*\}.\]
An exact algorithm must output some \(x^*\in X^*\), or correctly report \(X^*=\varnothing\) when \(F\equiv+\infty\). In the value-oracle model, one oracle call at \(x\) returns \(F(x)\); tractability statements must measure both oracle calls and auxiliary arithmetic as functions of \(|V|\), \(|L|\), and the encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multilabel minimization seeks a lowest-cost assignment from a finite label set, with complexity measured in the stated input or oracle model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An exact solution is any \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in L^V}F(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the minimization container, but the record is internally inconsistent: under its displayed definition, if F is identically +\infty then F^*=+\infty and X^*=L^V, not the empty set. A source is also absent, so the intended infeasibility convention cannot be determined reliably.

children.title: Tractable Label Regimes
children.top_down_role: Label structures associated with tractable minimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Tractable Label Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle tractability of fixed-label k-submodular minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(k\ge1\). Given a value oracle for a finite-valued \(k\)-submodular function \(f:D_k^V\to\mathbb Q\), an exact minimizer can be found using a number of oracle calls and rational arithmetic operations polynomial in \(|V|\) and the binary encoding length of the returned values. Thus the Boolean regime \(k=1\), the bisubmodular regime \(k=2\), and every fixed finite star-label regime belong to polynomial-time oracle minimization. This claim concerns functions satisfying the full \(k\)-submodular inequality, not arbitrary functions merely having \(k+1\) labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every fixed number of nonnull star labels, exact k-submodular minimization is polynomial-time in the value-oracle model.
assumptions_latex: Oracle values have finite binary encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D_k^V}f(x)\) is computable in oracle-polynomial time.

notation.meaning: Star domain with k nonnull labels and one null label.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A complexity bound is the correct role for the tractable-regime leaf, but the exact oracle-polynomial minimization theorem, its fixed-k restriction, and its dependence on returned-value encoding length require a theorem-level citation. None is supplied.

children.title: Multilabel Hardness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where multilabel minimization loses tractability.

knowledge_statements.title: Multilabel Hardness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardness once unrestricted pairwise three-label costs are admitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L=\{1,2,3\}\). For an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with terminals \(t_1,t_2,t_3\), consider
\[F(x)=\sum_{ij\in E}w_{ij}\mathbf 1[x_i\ne x_j]+\sum_{ell=1}^3M\mathbf 1[x_{t_ell}\ne\ell],\]
where \(w_{ij}\ge0\) and \(M>\sum_{ij\in E}w_{ij}\). Minimizing \(F\) is equivalent to the three-terminal multiway-cut problem and is NP-hard. Hence a finite label set and pairwise decomposition alone do not yield tractability; additional structure such as a suitable generalized submodularity inequality is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three-label pairwise minimization is already NP-hard: the Potts disagreement energy with fixed terminals encodes three-terminal multiway cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact minimization of this three-label energy family is NP-hard.

notation.meaning: Penalty forcing each terminal to its prescribed label.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and the three-terminal multiway-cut encoding fit this leaf. The forcing argument using M greater than the total edge weight is sound, but the NP-hardness premise and reduction require a specific authoritative theorem or section locator, which is absent.

children.title: Discrete Convex Analysis
children.top_down_role: Discrete convex sets and functions, their combinatorial origins, class hierarchy, polyhedral geometry, conjugacy, duality, optimization methods, and failure boundaries.

children.title: Quadratic Discrete Convex Functions
children.top_down_role: Quadratic function families arising in discrete convex analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Discrete Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic L-natural-convex functions on the integer lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A quadratic function \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\) of the form
\[f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Ax+b^{\mathsf T}x+c\]
is quadratic \(L^\natural\)-convex when \(A\) is symmetric, \(a_{ij}\le0\) for all distinct \(i,j\), and \(a_{ii}\ge\sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}|\) for every \(i\). Equivalently, its quadratic coefficients satisfy the discrete midpoint inequality
\[f(x)+f(y)\ge f(\lceil(x+y)/2\rceil)+f(\lfloor(x+y)/2\rfloor)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb Z^n),\]
where rounding is coordinatewise. The affine terms do not affect this convexity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lattice quadratic is L-natural-convex exactly when its symmetric quadratic matrix has nonpositive off-diagonal entries and is diagonally dominant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coefficient conditions imply the discrete midpoint inequality on \(\mathbb Z^n\).

notation.meaning: The discrete midpoint-convex class used in discrete convex analysis.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role is suitable, and the stated coefficient characterization is consistent with the usual quadratic L-natural-convex convention. Its if-and-only-if equivalence and the normalization using one half of x^T A x nevertheless require a precise source locator; none is supplied.

children.title: Symmetric M-Matrix Structure
children.top_down_role: Symmetric M-matrix structure relevant to quadratic discrete convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric M-Matrix Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonally dominant symmetric M-matrices used by lattice quadratics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) has the relevant symmetric M-matrix structure when
\[A=A^{\mathsf T},\qquad a_{ij}\le0\ \ (i\ne j),\qquad a_{ii}\ge\sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}|\ \ (i=1,\ldots,n).\]
Such a matrix is positive semidefinite. Indeed, writing \(r_i=a_{ii}+\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}\ge0\), its quadratic form has the decomposition
\[x^{\mathsf T}Ax=\sum_{i<j}(-a_{ij})(x_i-x_j)^2+\sum_i r_i x_i^2.\]
It is positive definite when this form vanishes only at \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relevant symmetric M-matrices are symmetric diagonally dominant matrices with nonpositive off-diagonal entries; their quadratic forms split into nonnegative difference terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is positive semidefinite and admits the displayed nonnegative quadratic-form decomposition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The matrix conditions define the symmetric diagonally dominant Z-matrix subclass relevant here, but “symmetric M-matrix” is broader or differently normalized in some sources. The paragraph beginning “Indeed” is proof text and must be removed from a knowledge statement. No source locator is supplied to settle the terminology.

children.title: Matrix–Function Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The structural interface between matrix conditions plus quadratic function classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix–Function Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient characterization of quadratic L-natural convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=	frac12x^{\mathsf T}Ax+b^{\mathsf T}x+c\) on \(\mathbb Z^n\), with \(A=A^{\mathsf T}\). Then \(f\) is \(L^
atural\)-convex if and only if \(A\) has nonpositive off-diagonal entries and is diagonally dominant:
\[a_{ij}\le0\quad(i
e j),\qquad a_{ii}\ge\sum_{j
e i}|a_{ij}|\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).\]
Consequently, the quadratic part of every such function is represented by a symmetric diagonally dominant M-matrix, while every matrix of this class, combined with arbitrary affine coefficients \(b,c\), defines an \(L^
atural\)-convex quadratic function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic L-natural-convex functions correspond exactly to symmetric diagonally dominant M-matrices, independently of their affine coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(L^\natural\)-convex if and only if \(A\) is a symmetric diagonally dominant M-matrix.

notation.meaning: Matrix representing the quadratic part of f.
Affine coefficients, unrestricted by L-natural convexity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is the correct content kind for this matrix-function correspondence, and the mathematical form is plausible under the symmetric diagonally dominant M-matrix convention. The exact equivalence and terminology require a specific theorem or proposition citation, which is absent.

children.title: Real-Valued Nonlinear Networks
children.top_down_role: Nonlinear network models over real-valued variables.

assumptions_latex: Each \(\varphi_e\) is proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed problem minimizes a separable convex objective over a convex real-flow feasible set.

notation.meaning: Proper closed convex cost on arc e.
Vector of node supplies and demands.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous separable convex-cost flow model; no unconditional attainment assertion is included.

source_refs.locator: Section 1.2.2, “Network Flow Problems with Convex Cost,” p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\). Given \(d\in\mathbb R^V\), bounds \(\ell_e,u_e\in\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}\) with \(\ell_e\le u_e\), and proper closed convex functions \(\varphi_e:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), a real-valued nonlinear network problem has the form
\[\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}\varphi_e(x_e):Bx=d,\ \ell_e\le x_e\le u_e\ \text{for every }e\in E,\ x\in\mathbb R^E\right\}.\]
Its feasible set is convex, and every attained local minimum is a global minimum. If the objective is strictly convex on the feasible set, the problem has at most one optimal flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued nonlinear network problem minimizes separable closed convex arc costs over real flows satisfying node balances and capacity bounds. Convexity makes any attained local minimum global, while strict convexity ensures uniqueness when an optimum exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Real-Valued Nonlinear Networks

assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb Z^V\), and the finite bounds among \(\ell,u\) are integral.
For every \(e\in E\), the effective domain of \(\psi_e\) is an integer interval and its forward differences are nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed problem minimizes a separable discrete-convex objective over integral flows satisfying the stated balance and bound constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with incidence matrix \(B\), let \(d\in\mathbb Z^V\), and let \(\ell,u\in(\mathbb Z\cup\{\pm\infty\})^E\) satisfy \(\ell_e\le u_e\) for every \(e\in E\). An integer-valued nonlinear network problem has the form
\[\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}\psi_e(x_e):Bx=d,\ \ell_e\le x_e\le u_e\ \text{for every }e\in E,\ x\in\mathbb Z^E\right\},\]
where each \(\psi_e:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is discrete convex: its effective domain \(\operatorname{dom}\psi_e=\{t\in\mathbb Z:\psi_e(t)<+\infty\}\) is an integer interval, and
\[\psi_e(t+1)-\psi_e(t)\le\psi_e(t+2)-\psi_e(t+1)\]
whenever \(t,t+1,t+2\in\operatorname{dom}\psi_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer-valued nonlinear network problem minimizes separable discrete-convex arc costs over integral flows with integral balances and bounds. Each extended-valued arc cost has an interval effective domain and nondecreasing forward differences.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Valued Nonlinear Networks

children.title: Network Integrality Transfer
children.top_down_role: Structural passage between real-valued plus integer-valued network models.

assumptions_latex: The directed network has node-arc incidence matrix \(A\), integral balance vector \(b\), and integral bounds \(\ell,u\).
Each arc cost \(\phi_a:[\ell_a,u_a]\to\mathbb R\) is convex piecewise linear with all breakpoints integral.
The feasible set \(\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) is nonempty and the minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is an optimal flow \(x^*\in\mathbb Z^E\), and the continuous and integer formulations have the same optimal value.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,E)\) be a directed network and minimize \(\sum_{a\in E}\phi_a(x_a)\) subject to \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\). Assume \(b,\ell,u\) are integral and every \(\phi_a\) is convex piecewise linear with integral breakpoints. If the feasible set is nonempty and the minimum is attained, then an optimal solution can be chosen in \(\mathbb Z^E\). Consequently,
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{a\in E}\phi_a(x_a):Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\right\}
=
\min\left\{\sum_{a\in E}\phi_a(x_a):Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u,\ x\in\mathbb Z^E\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral network data and convex piecewise-linear arc costs with integral breakpoints guarantee an integral optimum of the continuous flow formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Network Integrality Transfer

children.title: Network Substitution Effects
children.top_down_role: Substitutive interactions represented through network structure.

assumptions_latex: The interaction graph is \(G=(V,E)\), and \(F\) is defined on an integer box \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z^V\).
The valuation convention is used: larger \(F\) is preferred.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The network exhibits substitution effects when \(\Delta_{ij}F(x)\le 0\) for every admissible edge-coordinate increment.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise substitutes under the valuation, rather than cost, sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(ij\in E\) and every \(x\in B\) such that \(x+e_i\), \(x+e_j\), and \(x+e_i+e_j\) belong to \(B\), define
\[
\Delta_{ij}F(x)=F(x+e_i+e_j)-F(x+e_i)-F(x+e_j)+F(x).
\]
The valuation \(F:B\to\mathbb R\) has network substitution effects on \(G\) if
\[
\Delta_{ij}F(x)\le 0
\]
for every such \(ij\) and \(x\). Equivalently, increasing coordinate \(j\) weakly decreases the marginal value \(F(x+e_i)-F(x)\) of increasing coordinate \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adjacent coordinates are substitutes when increasing one never raises the discrete marginal value of increasing the other.
knowledge_statements.title: Network Substitution Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cross-difference condition correctly expresses pairwise substitutes under the stated valuation convention, but no source establishes that this is the intended network-specific terminology or convention for this taxonomy leaf.

children.title: Network Complementarity Effects
children.top_down_role: Complementary interactions represented through network structure.

assumptions_latex: The interaction graph is \(G=(V,E)\), and \(F\) is defined on an integer box \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z^V\).
The valuation convention is used: larger \(F\) is preferred.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The network exhibits complementarity effects when \(\Delta_{ij}F(x)\ge 0\) for every admissible edge-coordinate increment.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise complements under the valuation, rather than cost, sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(ij\in E\) and every \(x\in B\) such that \(x+e_i\), \(x+e_j\), and \(x+e_i+e_j\) belong to \(B\), define
\[
\Delta_{ij}F(x)=F(x+e_i+e_j)-F(x+e_i)-F(x+e_j)+F(x).
\]
The valuation \(F:B\to\mathbb R\) has network complementarity effects on \(G\) if
\[
\Delta_{ij}F(x)\ge 0
\]
for every such \(ij\) and \(x\). Equivalently, increasing coordinate \(j\) weakly increases the marginal value \(F(x+e_i)-F(x)\) of increasing coordinate \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adjacent coordinates are complements when increasing one never lowers the discrete marginal value of increasing the other.
knowledge_statements.title: Network Complementarity Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cross-difference condition correctly expresses pairwise complements under the stated valuation convention, but the network-specific terminology and sign convention have no cited support.

children.title: Mixed Network Interaction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interfaces where substitutive plus complementary behavior coexist.

assumptions_latex: The interaction graph is \(G=(V,E)\), and \(F\) is defined on an integer box \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z^V\).
The valuation convention is used, and all relevant cross-differences are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is mixed precisely when the admissible family \(\{\Delta_{ij}F(x)\}\) contains both a positive and a negative value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly mixed pairwise signs across edges or feasible network states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every edge \(ij\in E\) and feasible \(x\in B\), let
\[
\Delta_{ij}F(x)=F(x+e_i+e_j)-F(x+e_i)-F(x+e_j)+F(x),
\]
whenever all four arguments lie in \(B\). The network interaction regime of \(F\) is mixed if there exist admissible \((ij,x)\) and \((k\ell,y)\) such that
\[
\Delta_{ij}F(x)<0<\Delta_{k\ell}F(y).
\]
Thus the same model contains a substitution effect and a complementarity effect, possibly on different edges or at different feasible states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network regime is mixed when some admissible cross-difference is negative and another is positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Network Interaction Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement gives a coherent strict mixed-sign regime, but no source confirms that mixed network interactions must contain both a strictly negative and a strictly positive cross-difference rather than merely fail the uniform substitution and complementarity conditions.

children.title: Matroidal Domains
children.top_down_role: Matroid structures serving as domains for discrete convex models.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family \(\mathcal B\) is a matroidal domain exactly when it satisfies equicardinality and basis exchange.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: matroid bases are characterized by the basis-exchange axiom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matroidal domains represented as families of bases on a finite ground set.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty family \(\mathcal B\subseteq 2^E\) is a matroidal domain if all its members have the same cardinality and it satisfies basis exchange: for every \(X,Y\in\mathcal B\) and every \(i\in X\setminus Y\), there exists \(j\in Y\setminus X\) such that
\[
X-i+j=(X\setminus\{i\})\cup\{j\}\in\mathcal B.
\]
Equivalently, \(\mathcal B\) is the family of bases of a matroid on \(E\). Its incidence-vector realization is \(\{\chi_X:X\in\mathcal B\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^E\), whose vectors have a common coordinate sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroidal domain is a nonempty equicardinal family of subsets satisfying the basis-exchange axiom.
knowledge_statements.title: Matroidal Domains

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Valuated Matroids
children.top_down_role: Valued matroid structures within discrete convex analysis.

assumptions_latex: The effective domain \(\mathcal B=\{X:f(X)<+\infty\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(f\) is a valuated matroid when it satisfies the valuated basis-exchange inequality.

notation.meaning: Exchange of i for j in X

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real valuated matroids in the minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) with nonempty effective domain \(\mathcal B\) is a valuated matroid if, for all \(X,Y\in\mathcal B\) and each \(i\in X\setminus Y\), there exists \(j\in Y\setminus X\) such that
\[
f(X)+f(Y)\ge f(X-i+j)+f(Y-j+i).
\]
The inequality implies that both exchanged sets on the right belong to \(\mathcal B\); hence \(\mathcal B\) is a matroidal domain and all its sets have the same cardinality. Reversing the inequality gives the equivalent maximization convention for valuations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valuated matroid assigns extended-real weights to bases and satisfies a paired basis-exchange inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Valuated Matroids

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The extended-real minimization formulation and paired exchange inequality are mathematically coherent, but the precise valuated-matroid convention and its domain consequence require a direct authoritative citation.

children.title: Matroid Valuation Interface
children.top_down_role: The passage from unvalued matroid structure to valued exchange structure.

assumptions_latex: The function \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) has nonempty equicardinal effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Valuated matroids on \(E\) correspond exactly to \(M\)-convex functions supported on fixed-sum binary vectors.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary fixed-sum interface between valuated matroids and M-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), define \(g:\mathbb Z^E\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) by
\[
g(\chi_X)=f(X)\quad(X\subseteq E),\qquad g(x)=+\infty\quad(x\notin\{0,1\}^E).
\]
Then \(f\) is a valuated matroid in the minimization convention if and only if \(g\) is \(M\)-convex and \(\operatorname{dom}g\) lies in a fixed-sum hyperplane. Under this correspondence, basis exchange of sets becomes the \(M\)-exchange operation \(x-e_i+e_j\), and the matroidal domain of \(f\) becomes the binary effective domain of \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incidence-vector encoding identifies valuated matroids with M-convex functions whose finite domain consists of fixed-sum binary vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Valuation Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary incidence-vector representation is the appropriate kind of interface claim, but the exact equivalence with M-convexity and the role of the fixed-sum condition need a direct discrete-convex-analysis source.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair has the integral-intersection property exactly when every nonempty face of \(P\cap Q\) contains an integer point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic integrality criterion for the common feasible region of two rational polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For rational polyhedra \(P,Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), call \((P,Q)\) an integral pair when their common feasible region is integral:
\[
P\cap Q=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((P\cap Q)\cap\mathbb Z^n\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, every nonempty face \(F\) of \(P\cap Q\) contains an integer point. If \(P\cap Q\) is pointed, this is also equivalent to every vertex of \(P\cap Q\) being integral. Integrality of \(P\) and \(Q\) separately is not part of this definition and, without an additional structural hypothesis, does not imply integrality of their intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two rational polyhedra form an integral pair when their intersection is the convex hull of its integer points.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality for Pairs of Polyhedra

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated face characterization is plausible for an integral rational intersection, but no source confirms that the taxonomy's 'pair' terminology means only integrality of the intersection. A source is also needed to determine whether this leaf should contain a definition, condition, or stronger structural theorem.

children.title: Integrally Convex Sets
children.top_down_role: The set-level component of integral convexity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(S\) is integrally convex when every point of \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is generated by nearby points of \(S\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: local-neighborhood convex-hull definition is standard in discrete convex analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard local-neighborhood definition for subsets of the integer lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), define its integral neighborhood by
\[
N(x)=\{z\in\mathbb Z^n:|z_i-x_i|<1\text{ for every }i\}.
\]
A nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) is integrally convex if
\[
x\in\operatorname{conv}(S\cap N(x))
\]
for every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\). Thus each point of the global convex hull must admit a convex representation using only lattice points of \(S\) lying in the unit cell or cells incident to that point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lattice set is integrally convex when every point of its convex hull is a convex combination of neighboring set points.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrally Convex Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local-neighborhood definition is standard and internally consistent, but the record provides no inspectable citation with a section, definition, theorem, or page locator.

children.title: Local Convex Hulls
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood-scale hull geometry for lattice sets.

assumptions_latex: The set \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) and point \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local convex hull at \(x\) is \(\operatorname{conv}(S\cap N(x))\), and it is contained in \(\operatorname{conv}S\).

notation.meaning: Local convex hull of S at x

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convex hull of lattice points in the integral neighborhood
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local hull generated by lattice points in the open unit coordinate neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), let
\[
N(x)=\{z\in\mathbb Z^n:|z_i-x_i|<1\text{ for all }i\}.
\]
The local convex hull of \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) at \(x\) is
\[
L_S(x)=\operatorname{conv}(S\cap N(x)).
\]
It is a polytope, possibly empty, generated by at most \(2^n\) lattice points and satisfies \(L_S(x)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}S\). When \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\), the strict inequalities give \(N(x)=\{x\}\), so \(L_S(x)=\{x\}\) if \(x\in S\) and is empty otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local hull at a point is the convex hull of set points lying in that point's integral neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Convex Hulls

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local-hull definition and its elementary boundary cases are consistent, but no authoritative citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Local-Hull Characterization
children.top_down_role: The relationship between integral convexity plus local hull structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(S\) is integrally convex if and only if \(\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{x\in\operatorname{conv}S}\operatorname{conv}(S\cap N(x))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise and union forms of the local-hull characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be nonempty and set \(L_S(x)=\operatorname{conv}(S\cap N(x))\). The following are equivalent:
\[
\text{(i) }S\text{ is integrally convex};
\]
\[
\text{(ii) }x\in L_S(x)\text{ for every }x\in\operatorname{conv}S;
\]
\[
\text{(iii) }\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{x\in\operatorname{conv}S}L_S(x).
\]
Indeed, each local hull is automatically contained in \(\operatorname{conv}S\); the substantive condition is that every point of the global hull belongs to its own local hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral convexity is equivalent to every global-hull point lying in its own local hull, or to local hulls covering the global hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Hull Characterization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem content kind fits the characterization leaf, and the three formulations are presented consistently, but the equivalence—particularly the union formulation—requires a direct source with a specific locator.

children.title: Integrally Convex Functions
children.top_down_role: The function-level component of integral convexity.

assumptions_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) has nonempty effective domain.
The local convex extension is formed from finite convex combinations over each integral neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(f\) is integrally convex exactly when its local convex extension \(\widetilde f\) is convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convexity of the local convex extension is the standard definition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real lattice functions defined through convexity of their local convex extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(N(x)=\{z\in\mathbb Z^n:|z_i-x_i|<1\text{ for all }i\}\) and define
\[
\widetilde f(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{z\in N(x)}\lambda_z f(z):\lambda_z\ge0,\ \sum_z\lambda_z=1,\ \sum_z\lambda_z z=x\right\},
\]
with value \(+\infty\) when no finite feasible combination exists. The function \(f\) is integrally convex if its local convex extension \(\widetilde f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is convex. At every lattice point \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\), one has \(N(x)=\{x\}\) and therefore \(\widetilde f(x)=f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lattice function is integrally convex when interpolation by convex combinations within each integral neighborhood produces a globally convex extension.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrally Convex Functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected definition matches the standard role of integrally convex functions, but no direct source is cited. The infimum formula should also explicitly restrict positive-weight support to finite-valued lattice points, avoiding undefined products involving zero weights and +infinity.

children.title: Local Convex Extensions
children.top_down_role: Local continuous extensions associated with lattice functions.

assumptions_latex: For each \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), convex combinations are taken over the finite set \(N(x)=\{z\in\mathbb{Z}^n\mid \lfloor x_i\rfloor\le z_i\le\lceil x_i\rceil\ \text{for all }i\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed optimization defines \(\widetilde f\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: integer points in the smallest coordinatewise unit box containing x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local convex closure over each coordinatewise unit cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the local convex extension of \(f\) is
\[
\widetilde f(x)=\min\left\{\sum_{z\in N(x)}\lambda_z f(z)\ \middle|\ \lambda_z\ge0,\ \sum_{z\in N(x)}\lambda_z=1,\ \sum_{z\in N(x)}\lambda_z z=x\right\}.
\]
Terms with \(\lambda_z=0\) contribute zero even when \(f(z)=+\infty\); equivalently, only points with finite function value may receive positive weight. If no admissible finite-valued convex combination exists, the minimum is \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local convex extension linearly convexifies the lattice values separately inside every coordinatewise unit cell.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Convex Extensions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied for the extended-valued local-extension convention.

children.title: Local-Extension Fidelity
children.top_down_role: How local extensions preserve or fail to preserve integral convexity.

assumptions_latex: The local convex extension \(\widetilde f\) is formed from \(f:\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) using coordinatewise unit-cell neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), \(\widetilde f(x)=f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery of lattice data by the local convex extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an integer point \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), its unit-cell neighborhood is the singleton \(N(x)=\{x\}\). Consequently, the only coefficients satisfying \(\lambda_z\ge0\), \(\sum_z\lambda_z=1\), and \(\sum_z\lambda_z z=x\) have \(\lambda_x=1\). Hence the local convex extension preserves every original lattice value:
\[
\widetilde f(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb{Z}^n).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every lattice point, the local convex extension agrees exactly with the original function.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Extension Fidelity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fidelity property is standard and correctly typed, but it has no citation and the statement includes a derivation that should not appear in proof-free knowledge text.

children.title: M-Convex Sets
children.top_down_role: Set geometry specific to the M-convex class.

assumptions_latex: The set \(S\) is a nonempty subset of \(\mathbb{Z}^n\).
The vectors \(e_i\) are the standard unit vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exchange predicate in the statement defines an M-convex set.

notation.meaning: indices where x is below y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer exchange-axiom definition of an M-convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) is M-convex if, for every \(x,y\in S\) and every \(i\in\operatorname{supp}^{+}(x-y)\), there exists \(j\in\operatorname{supp}^{-}(x-y)\) such that
\[
x-e_i+e_j\in S\quad\text{and}\quad y+e_i-e_j\in S.
\]
This exchange axiom implies that all vectors in \(S\) have the same component sum, because otherwise an excess coordinate could not always be paired with a deficit coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M-convex set permits every unit removed from an excess coordinate to be exchanged with some deficit coordinate in both compared vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: M-Convex Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exchange-axiom definition and content kind fit the node, but neither the definition nor the appended constant-sum assertion has cited support.

children.title: M-Natural-Convex Sets
children.top_down_role: Set geometry specific to the M-natural-convex class.

assumptions_latex: The set \(S\) is a nonempty subset of \(\mathbb{Z}^n\).
The vectors \(e_i\) are the standard unit vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The alternative exchange predicate in the statement defines an M-natural-convex set.

notation.meaning: indices where x is below y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer exchange definition allowing transfer without a compensating coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) is M-natural-convex if, for every \(x,y\in S\) and every \(i\in\operatorname{supp}^{+}(x-y)\), either
\[
x-e_i\in S\quad\text{and}\quad y+e_i\in S,
\]
or there exists \(j\in\operatorname{supp}^{-}(x-y)\) such that
\[
x-e_i+e_j\in S\quad\text{and}\quad y+e_i-e_j\in S.
\]
Unlike M-convexity, this axiom permits component sums to vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M-natural-convex set allows either a direct unit transfer or a paired exchange through a deficit coordinate.
knowledge_statements.title: M-Natural-Convex Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated alternative exchange axiom is plausible and belongs in this definition leaf, but no authoritative source with a precise locator is provided.

children.title: M-Type Set Translation
children.top_down_role: Structural passage between the two M-type set classes.

assumptions_latex: A fixed integer \(r\) is used for the added coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(S\) is M-natural-convex if and only if \(\widehat S_r\) is M-convex.

notation.meaning: sum of the coordinates of x
constant-sum lift of S into one additional coordinate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-sum lifting equivalence between the two M-type set classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the constant-sum lift
\[
\widehat S_r=\{(r-x(N),x)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}\mid x\in S\}.
\]
Then \(S\) is M-natural-convex if and only if \(\widehat S_r\) is M-convex. An exchange involving the added coordinate corresponds exactly to the direct-transfer alternative in the M-natural exchange axiom; an exchange between two original coordinates corresponds to its paired-exchange alternative. The equivalence holds for every choice of \(r\in\mathbb{Z}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a coordinate that fixes the total sum converts M-natural-convex sets exactly into M-convex sets.
knowledge_statements.title: M-Type Set Translation

children.title: M-Convex Functions
children.top_down_role: Function structure specific to the M-convex class.

assumptions_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) has nonempty effective domain.
The vectors \(e_i\) are the standard unit vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The four-point exchange inequality in the statement defines an M-convex function.

notation.meaning: indices where x is below y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued integer exchange-inequality definition of M-convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is M-convex if, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(i\in\operatorname{supp}^{+}(x-y)\), there exists \(j\in\operatorname{supp}^{-}(x-y)\) such that
\[
f(x)+f(y)\ge f(x-e_i+e_j)+f(y+e_i-e_j).
\]
In particular, the points on the right belong to \(\operatorname{dom}f\), so the effective domain of an M-convex function is an M-convex set and therefore has constant component sum.

children.title: M-Natural-Convex Functions
children.top_down_role: Function structure specific to the M-natural-convex class.

assumptions_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) has nonempty effective domain.
The vectors \(e_i\) are the standard unit vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The alternative exchange inequality in the statement defines an M-natural-convex function.

notation.meaning: indices where x is below y

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is M-natural-convex if, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(i\in\operatorname{supp}^{+}(x-y)\), either
\[
f(x)+f(y)\ge f(x-e_i)+f(y+e_i),
\]
or there exists \(j\in\operatorname{supp}^{-}(x-y)\) such that
\[
f(x)+f(y)\ge f(x-e_i+e_j)+f(y+e_i-e_j).
\]
The effective domain is consequently an M-natural-convex set.

children.title: M-Type Function Translation
children.top_down_role: Structural passage between the two M-type function classes.

assumptions_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) has nonempty effective domain.
A fixed integer \(r\) is used for the added coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(f\) is M-natural-convex if and only if \(\widehat f_r\) is M-convex.

notation.meaning: sum of the coordinates of x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-sum lifting equivalence between M-natural-convex and M-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(\widehat f_r:\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) by
\[
\widehat f_r(x_0,x)=
\begin{cases}
f(x),&x_0+x(N)=r,\\+\infty,&x_0+x(N)\ne r.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f\) is M-natural-convex if and only if \(\widehat f_r\) is M-convex. Exchanges through coordinate \(0\) encode direct unit transfers, while exchanges among coordinates \(1,\ldots,n\) encode paired exchanges. This equivalence is independent of the chosen \(r\in\mathbb{Z}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant-sum auxiliary coordinate translates M-natural-convex functions exactly into M-convex functions.

children.title: Local Exchange Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Local neighborhoods generated by M-type exchange structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local exchange neighborhood of \(x\) is \(\mathcal N_f(x)\) as displayed.

notation.meaning: standard unit vector in coordinate i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible unit exchanges for an M-convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), its local exchange neighborhood is
\[
\mathcal N_f(x)=\{x-e_i+e_j\mid i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\ f(x-e_i+e_j)<+\infty\}.
\]
Allowing \(i=j\) includes \(x\) itself. A strict descent move is any \(y\in\mathcal N_f(x)\) satisfying \(f(y)<f(x)\); thus every local move preserves the component sum and changes at most two coordinates by one unit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local neighborhood consists of all feasible vectors obtained by moving one unit from one coordinate to another.

children.title: Descent Certificates
